title: Question 2
stem:
A small block is lifted vertically upwards by a toy aircraft, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1

As the block is moving upwards, the string breaks at time $t = 0$. The block initially continues moving upwards and then falls and hits the ground at time $t = 0.90\,\text{s}$. The variation with time $t$ of the velocity $v$ of the block is shown in Fig. 2.2.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

Fig. 2.2

Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the feature of the graph in Fig. 2.2 that shows the block has a constant acceleration.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the slope or gradient of a velocity-time graph represents physically.
parts.proper_answer: The graph is a straight line with constant gradient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Gradient to Acceleration**
On a velocity-time graph, acceleration is the gradient, $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$. If acceleration is constant, the rate of change of velocity is the same at every instant.

Step 2: **Read the Shape in Fig. 2.2**
Fig. 2.2 is a single straight line from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.90\text{ s}$. A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the acceleration is constant and downwards.

enrichment.proper_answer: The graph is a straight line with constant gradient.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use Fig. 2.2 to determine the height of the block above the ground when the string breaks at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: Remember that area between the v-t graph and the time axis gives displacement, with areas above and below the axis having opposite signs.
Hint 2: Split the motion at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$ where $v = 0$ and work out the small upward triangle and the large downward triangle separately.
Hint 3: Relate the downward area to the upward distance plus the initial height $H$ above the ground to solve for $H$.
parts.proper_answer: Upward displacement $= \frac{1}{2} \times 1.96 \times 0.20 = 0.196\text{ m}$. Downward displacement magnitude $= \frac{1}{2} \times 6.86 \times 0.70 = 2.401\text{ m}$. Height $= 2.401 - 0.196 = 2.2\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Area as Displacement**
You are sitting beside me, so let's picture it. The block first coasts up, stops, then falls to the ground. On a $v$-$t$ graph, displacement is area under the graph. Area above the $t$-axis is upward displacement, area below is downward displacement.

Step 2: **Calculate the Two Triangular Areas**
Upward motion is $0$ to $0.20\text{ s}$: $$\text{area}_{up} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.20 \times 1.96 = 0.196\text{ m}$$ Downward motion is $0.20\text{ s}$ to $0.90\text{ s}$, so time falling $= 0.70\text{ s}$: $$\text{area}_{down} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.70 \times 6.86 = 2.401\text{ m}$$

Step 3: **Find the Starting Height**
The downward area covers first the $0.196\text{ m}$ back down to the break point, then the extra height $H$ to the ground. So: $$H = \text{area}_{down} - \text{area}_{up} = 2.401 - 0.196 = 2.205\text{ m} \approx 2.2\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The block has a weight of $0.86\,\text{N}$.

Calculate the difference in gravitational potential energy of the block between time $t = 0$ and time $t = 0.90\,\text{s}$.

markscheme_points.guidance: alternative methods are possible using equations of motion

hints: Hint 1: Recall how loss of height relates to loss of gravitational potential energy when weight rather than mass is given.
Hint 2: Use your height from (b) as the vertical drop from $t = 0$ to the ground at $t = 0.90\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the Energy Formula**
Change in gravitational potential energy is weight times change in vertical height, $$\Delta E_p = W \Delta h$$, because $W = mg$. Here the block ends on the ground, so $\Delta h$ is just the starting height from (b).

Step 2: **Substitute and Calculate**
$$\Delta E_p = 0.86 \times 2.2 = 1.892\text{ J} \approx 1.9\text{ J}$$ This is a decrease, the energy is transferred to kinetic energy as it falls.

parts.label: (d)

markscheme_points.text: gradient of curved line decreases and is zero at $t = 0.90\ \text{s}$

hints: Hint 1: Think about what distance means here - it keeps increasing as long as the block moves, even while it slows down going up.
Hint 2: Think about how the gradient of a distance-time graph behaves when speed is steadily decreasing to zero at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$.
parts.proper_answer: Curved line starting at the origin with decreasing positive gradient, becoming horizontal (zero gradient) at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start From the Origin With a Curve**
Distance moved starts at zero at $t = 0$ and can only increase. Because speed is changing, the graph cannot be straight, it must be curved. So draw a curve leaving the origin going upwards.

Step 2: **Make the Gradient Decrease to Zero**
Gradient of a distance-time graph is speed. The block is slowing down as it rises, with velocity falling from $1.96\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to zero at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$. So the curve gets flatter and flatter and is horizontal at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text:
A block of greater mass is now released from the same height with the same upward velocity. Air resistance is still negligible.

State and explain the effect, if any, of the increased mass on the speed with which the block hits the ground.

markscheme_points.text: acceleration (of free fall) is unchanged / is not dependent on mass

hints: Hint 1: Consider what determines acceleration when the only force is weight and air resistance can be ignored.
parts.proper_answer: No effect on impact speed. Acceleration of free fall $g$ is unchanged and independent of mass.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See Why Mass Cancels Out**
With no air resistance the only force is weight $W = mg$, so by $F = ma$, $$a = \frac{mg}{m} = g$$. A larger mass has larger weight but also larger inertia by the same factor, so $g$ is the same. Released from the same height with the same initial velocity, the time of flight and final speed are unchanged.
